definition: Transdermal optical imaging, also known as transdermal optical imagery or TOI, is a method of detecting blood flow of the face by measuring hemoglobin concentration using a digital video camera.
details: Because of the translucent property of skin, light can travel beneath the skin and re-emit. The re-emitted light from underneath the skin is affected by chromophores, mainly hemoglobin and melanin, which differ in color. The color difference allows TOI machine learning software to separate the images into layers, which are known as bitplanes. It extracts signals rich in hemoglobin and signals rich in melanin, then discards the melanin-rich signals to obtain a recording of hemoglobin changes under the skin. Transdermal optical imaging has been proposed as an alternative to cuff-based methods of measuring blood pressure because it is able to measure heart rate accurately in a "contactless and non-invasive" way. Transdermal optical imaging may be able to detect hidden emotions using the patterns of blood flow in the face.

explainer.lead: Transdermal optical imaging (TOI) estimates facial blood flow by measuring hemoglobin concentration from ordinary digital video. It offers a contactless way to capture physiological signal from a camera rather than a sensor on the skin.

tiers.eli5: Your skin lets a little light pass through. A camera can see the faint color change from the blood underneath, much like noticing someone's face flush.
tiers.practitioner: Pipelines separate re-emitted light into bitplanes, keep the hemoglobin-rich signal and discard the melanin-rich one, since melanin color confounds the reading. A common pitfall is treating this melanin separation as trivial when skin tone varies.
tiers.paperLevel: Light travels beneath the translucent skin and re-emits; chromophores, mainly hemoglobin and melanin, alter its color. Software splits images into layers called bitplanes and extracts hemoglobin-rich versus melanin-rich signals, discarding the latter to record hemoglobin change.

explainer.example: A video camera records a face; the software splits the frames into bitplanes, extracts the hemoglobin-rich signal, and discards the melanin-rich signal to record hemoglobin changes.
